11 A car has mass m. A person needs to push the car with force F in order to give the car
acceleration a. The person needs to push the car with force 2F in order to give the car
acceleration 3a.
Which expression gives the constant resistive force opposing the motion of the car?
A
ma
B
2ma
C
3ma
D
4ma

hints: Notice the resultant force is not $F$ or $2F$ because a constant resistive force $R$ opposes each push.
Apply $F_{net} = ma$ to each case: $F - R = ma$ for push $F$ and acceleration $a$, and $2F - R = 3ma$ for push $2F$ and acceleration $3a$.
Subtract the first equation from the second to eliminate $R$ and find $F$ in terms of $ma$, then substitute back to find $R$.
walkthrough: Identify the two situations: push $F$ produces acceleration $a$, and push $2F$ produces acceleration $3a$, both with the same mass $m$ and same resistive force $R$.
State the rule: resultant force in direction of motion equals push minus resistance, and equals mass times acceleration, so $F_{net} = F_{push} - R = ma$.
Set up the two equations: $F - R = ma$ and $2F - R = m(3a) = 3ma$.
Subtract the first equation from the second: $(2F - R) - (F - R) = 3ma - ma$, which simplifies to $F = 2ma$.
Substitute $F = 2ma$ into $F - R = ma$ to get $2ma - R = ma$, so $R = 2ma - ma = ma$.
The resistive force $ma$ matches the expression listed. This is option A

A.explanation: Solving $F - R = ma$ and $2F - R = 3ma$ gives $F = 2ma$ and $R = F - ma = ma$.

B.explanation: This is the value of the push $F$, not the resistive force $R = F - ma$.

C.explanation: This is the resultant force $3ma$ in the second case, not the resistive force opposing the push.

D.explanation: This overestimates $R$ by ignoring that part of $F$ and $2F$ provides the $ma$ and $3ma$ resultant forces.
